newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Swiss Novartis reassures, sees strong growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swiss Novartis reassures, sees strong growth.

text.p: Swiss drugs and agricultural chemicals giant Novartis AG reported 1996 results in line with expectations on Tuesday and reassured investors that its merger was proceeding smoothly.

The company also said a sales boost of up to 12 percent from the weaker Swiss franc and annual costs savings, expected to reach two billion Swiss francs by 1999, were likely to lead to "a marked improvement in operating and net income" in 1997.

Novartis's senior management team travelled to London to present the results, the first since its formation through the merger of Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz last year which made it the world's second biggest drugs company behind Britain's Glaxo Wellcome Plc.

Novartis reported 1996 group net profit of 2.304 billion Swiss francs ($1.6 billion) versus 4.216 billion in 1995, including net exceptional charges of 1.9 billion francs. Shareholders were rewarded with a 19 percent hike in the annual dividend to 20 Swiss francs and promises of more to come.

In an interview with Reuters, Novartis President Daniel Vasella said the decision to increase the dividend payout to 33 percent of group net income was to bring the group in line with its international peers and return value to shareholders.
He ruled out a share buyback until Swiss law made it more tax advantageous.

Vasella said he did not believe the recent wave of mega-mergers in the drugs industry, which led to the birth of Novartis, had run its course, but said Novartis's strong balance sheet would not tempt it to rush into further acquisitions.

The group's robust cash flow and net liquidity "gives us the freedom strategically we need to act if we think something is attractive. But obviously it would be a mistake to feel pressured because you have money to rush in to an acquisiiton."

And Vasella added: "We want to be a leader in the fields we compete in, and we want to be at the forefront of innovation and to have a solid and forceful market presence, so it is important to be in the major league. But to be number one, two or three that really doesn't matter at all."

Analysts had largely discounted the results and were eager for news of progress in integrating the two companies and details of the drugs pipeline. Much of its existing product range is mature and facing generic competition.
The company said it hoped to achieve 60 percent of its cost savings in the current year, and said its planned headcount reduction was "on target."

"This will take some of the uncertainty out of the share (price)," said Gerd Ramsperger, head of brokerage research at Zuercher Kantonalbank. Novartis's registered shares closed barely changed on the day, down one franc at 1,739.

The group also revealed that it had 85 projects in clinical development, and planned 29 product launches in the next three years, dwarfing the 20 launches promised by rival Glaxo Wellcome over the next four years.

Novartis estimated that some 20 to 25 percent of its drug sales last year, which totaled 12.18 billion Swiss francs, came from products launched in the past five years. Vasella singled out anti-fungal treatment Lamisil, cholesterol-lowering agent Lescol and anti-hypertensive Cibacen/Lotensin as up-and-coming stars.
And further ahead he highlighted the promise of a number of drugs in development, including treatments for Alzheimer's disease, cancer, diabetes and irritable bowel syndrome.
Novartis said last year's sales in the core "life sciences" business -- pharmaceuticals, agribusiness and nutrition -- rose eight percent to 27.60 billion francs.
Total sales including the divested Ciba Specialty Chemicals rose to 36.23 billion francs from 35.94 billion. Operating income rose four percent.

Group research and development (R&D) spending rose by four percent, with R&D spending in the pharmaceutical sector held at 19 percent of sales, one of the highest in the industry. = 1.459 Swiss Francs)
